title: We Looked at America's 5 Most Haunted Roads by Satellite. We're Still Not Driving Them After Dark
excerpt: We checked America's five most haunted roads on satellite, from Clinton Road to old Highway 666. From above, a haunted road looks exactly like a road. The post We Looked at America’s 5 Most Haunted Ro...
content:
Two years ago we ranked America's most haunted roads, and you people ate it up. This time we skipped the gas money and pulled all five up on satellite. Spoiler: from above, a haunted road looks exactly like a road. Whatever's out there doesn't show up at this resolution.

5. Prospector's Road – Coloma, California

Prospector's Road (Prospectors Rd), off Marshall Road near Coloma in El Dorado County, California, comes with a claim dispute attached. The legend says a miner killed over his claim never left it. Drivers say a shadowy figure steps out of the brush with one warning: get off my claim.

4. The Devil's Promenade – Hornet, Missouri

For decades, witnesses have reported a floating light, the Hornet Spook Light, drifting over this road near the Oklahoma-Missouri border and changing color and shape as it goes. Some say it's two lovers still searching for each other. Others blame seismic activity or swamp gas. Skeptics have an answer: studies going back to the 1940s trace it to distant Route 66 headlights. Believers have heard that one.

3. Route 2A – Haynesville, Maine

Route 2A doesn't need ghosts. Winter in that part of Maine does plenty on its own. Locals tell of a young woman frantically waving for help who vanishes the moment you pull over, plus a small girl walking the shoulder alone in the dark. Nothing keeps a ghost story alive like a road where the nearest help is a long walk away.

2. Clinton Road – West Milford, New Jersey

Clinton Road has a resume: alleged mob dumping ground, paranormal hotspot, and supposed home of the ghost boy under the bridge. Toss a coin into the water, the story goes, and he'll throw it back. Then there are the phantom trucks. Drivers say headlights come out of nowhere and run them off the road. Naturally, people now drive out there on purpose.

1. Highway 666 (now U.S. Route 491) – Four Corners

Once officially numbered 666, this desert highway through Utah, Colorado, and New Mexico didn't need much help getting called the "Devil's Highway." Local lore includes hell hounds that shred tires and a red semi driven by something that isn't a trucker. On the record: a lonely desert highway, a bad crash history, and a number nobody wanted on the sign. It was renumbered 491 in 2003, partly to shake the reputation. The stories didn't change with the signs.

Drive them after dark if you like. We'll be home with the satellite view.

Which haunted road did we miss, and what actually happened the night you drove it? Details, please. 'It felt weird' doesn't count.
